Maya Angelou. The autobiographer, poet, and performer who became known as one of the most beloved and influential writers of her generation. Her memoir I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, published in 1969, recounts her journey overcoming poverty, racism, trauma, and mutism, making it a bestseller and a cornerstone of American autobiography.

The title of that work draws from Paul Laurence Dunbar's poem and uses the metaphor of a caged bird struggling toward freedom, applicable to both her own experience and her race's experience under oppression. I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings details her childhood in the segregated South and her temporary mutism after witnessing trauma, then traces her journey toward voice and self-acceptance. After this first volume, Angelou published six more volumes of autobiography continuing her life story across decades, making autobiography itself a form of resistance and witness. Her life itself embodied the multifaceted resilience her work celebrates—she worked as a dancer, actress, streetcar conductor, and journalist before becoming a writer.

Her poetry collections, including Just Give Me a Cool Drink of Water Before I Die, published in 1971, brought lyrical depth and vernacular language to meditations on love, racism, and redemption. She became a cultural icon and public intellectual, using her platform to advocate for civil rights, women's dignity, and the power of literature. Her legacy connects her to Langston Hughes, whose example of bringing vernacular into literature influenced her voice, and to Alice Walker and other contemporary writers centered on Black women's survival and self-affirmation.
